concepts.name: Uses of electricity, safety and the torchlight
concepts.description: Everyday uses of electricity, sources of electricity, safety cautions and the parts of a torchlight.
concepts.idea: Electricity has many uses; we experiment only with cells for safety.
concepts.rule: Electricity is used for lighting, cooking, heating and cooling, entertainment, communication, transportation and other work. Electricity is generated by windmills, solar panels, falling water and natural gas or coal, and reaches homes through wires. The Bhakra Nangal Dam uses falling water to generate electricity. Danger signs warn that electricity can be dangerous; never perform experiments with power supply at home or school, and use only cells such as those in torchlights, clocks and remotes. A torchlight has a lamp, a switch and two or more electric cells inside. The lamp glows in one position of the switch and not in the other.
concepts.example: Nihal grouped uses such as a fan, refrigerator and geyser under heating and cooling.

concepts.name: The electric cell and the battery
concepts.description: Terminals of a cell, how cells are joined to make a battery and why more cells are used.
concepts.idea: A cell has two terminals, and cells joined positive to negative form a battery.
concepts.rule: An electric cell is a portable source of electrical energy with two terminals: the metal cap is the positive (+) terminal and the flat metal disc is the negative (-) terminal. In a torch two cells must be placed in the correct order for the lamp to glow: the positive terminal of one cell is connected to the negative terminal of the next. Such a combination of two or more cells is called a battery. Connecting more than one cell gives energy for a longer time or more energy. The word battery is also used for a single cell, as in a mobile phone. In a device with cells side by side a metal strip joins the positive of one to the negative of the next, and + and - symbols show the placement.
concepts.example: Reversing one cell in a torch makes the lamp stop glowing.

concepts.name: Electric lamps: incandescent and LED
concepts.description: The filament lamp, its terminals, why a lamp fuses, and LEDs which have no filament and a direction.
concepts.idea: An incandescent lamp glows through a hot filament, while an LED has no filament and works in one direction.
concepts.rule: An incandescent lamp has a thin wire called the filament inside a glass bulb; when current passes it gets hot and glows to produce light. The filament is held by two thicker wires that connect to the metal case at the base and the metal tip at the centre; these are the two terminals and do not touch each other. A lamp that does not glow though connected is said to have 'fused', usually due to a broken filament that stops the current. Many torches now use a Light Emitting Diode (LED) lamp. An LED has no filament and two terminals: the longer wire is positive and the shorter wire is negative. An LED glows only when its positive terminal is connected to the positive of the battery.

concepts.name: Electrical circuit and switch
concepts.description: A complete circuit, direction of current, closed and open circuits, and the switch.
concepts.idea: A lamp glows only when a complete path lets current flow, and a switch opens or closes the path.
concepts.rule: A lamp glows when one terminal of the lamp is connected to one terminal of the cell and the other to the other terminal. This setup forms an electrical circuit, a complete path for current. The lamp glows only when current passes. The direction of electric current in a circuit is taken to be from the positive to the negative terminal of the cell. A switch is a simple device that completes or breaks a circuit; in the ON position the circuit is closed and current flows, and in the OFF position there is a gap and the circuit is open. A switch can be placed anywhere in a circuit. A simple switch can be made with drawing pins, a safety pin and a piece of cardboard.
concepts.example: A home switch works the same way as a simple safety pin switch.

concepts.name: Circuit diagrams and symbols
concepts.description: Symbols for electrical components and how to draw circuit diagrams.
concepts.idea: Symbols let us draw and read circuits simply and the same way all over the world.
concepts.rule: The components of an electrical circuit can be represented by symbols: cell, battery, lamp, LED, wire and switch in ON and OFF positions. In the symbol for an electric cell the long line is the positive terminal and the short line is the negative terminal. In the symbol for an LED the triangle points in the direction in which current can flow and the two arrows show that it emits light. A representation of a circuit using symbols is a circuit diagram. International organisations such as the IEC, ANSI and IEEE create standard symbols so people in different countries and industries understand each other easily. Circuit diagrams of a lamp with a switch and an LED with a battery can be drawn from the activities.
concepts.example: In a cell symbol the long line stands for the positive terminal.

concepts.name: Conductors, insulators and electrical safety
concepts.description: Materials that let current pass or not, why wires are metal and covered, DC and AC, and safety.
concepts.idea: Conductors let current pass and insulators do not, and both are used to make electricity safe and useful.
concepts.rule: A conduction tester made with a cell and a lamp with free wire ends shows whether a material lets current pass. Materials through which current flows easily are good conductors; those through which it does not are insulators or poor conductors. Metals are conductors; silver, copper and gold are the best, but copper is mainly used for wires due to lower cost and abundant supply. Plastic, rubber, glass, wood and ceramics are insulators, used to cover wires, plug tops and switches to protect people from electric shocks. Our body is a conductor, so never touch switches or plugs with wet hands or use damaged equipment. Cells give Direct Current (DC) for small devices, while the wall socket gives Alternating Current (AC) for larger appliances. Cells come as cylindrical, button and rechargeable types.
concepts.example: Keys, coins and spoons make the tester lamp glow, but wood and plastic do not.

questions.q: Why is safety with electricity so important? Give reasons.
questions.a: Electric current through the body can cause serious injury or death, so handling carefully protects lives.

questions.q: Make a list of household objects that are only insulators, only conductors and both.
questions.a: For example: rubber slippers, steel spoons, and a plug with metal pins and plastic body.
